title: The conquerors
hookLine: emperors who conquered every land, with drums beating, also went without the Name (Savaiye)

lines: NAGARAS IN FRONT OF THE MARCH.
cards: Before you see an army in the old world, you hear it. A low thudding comes over the hills, then another and another, until the ground itself seems to beat.

Kettledrums, war drums, the big nagaras, carried in front of the march so every village knows who's coming. Kings had them beaten when they set out and again when they came home with a new country in their pocket.
Now listen for the moment after the march has passed, when the last beat rolls away down the valley.

teach.b: Among the ten savaiye is a verse made of that sound. In paraphrase: they went out and conquered every land in every direction, with drums and kettledrums beating.
Their elephants trumpeted, their horses neighed by the thousand. Kings like these, past, present and to come, can't be counted.

teach.h: WITHOUT THE NAME, THEY STILL WENT.
teach.b: Then the turn the savaiye keep making: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home.
Beside it stands another savaiya, about warriors in shining armor so sure of themselves they thought even mountains couldn't move them. They too go. The striking thing is the man writing it.

Guru Gobind Singh had a great drum of his own. Sikh tradition remembers the Ranjit Nagara, a huge kettledrum made at Anandpur, beaten morning and evening, whose boom worried the hill kings around him.
Sikhs still beat a nagara at some gurdwaras and in processions today. So this isn't someone who hated drums; he knew how good it felt to hear your own. The verse's point is simpler and harder.

teach.h: VICTORY IS REAL, AND IT FADES.
teach.b: The sound of victory is real, and it fades.

The conquerors are measured not by how far their drums carried, but by whether they remembered the One who outlasts every march. In the Sikh view, that remembering, simran, is what keeps sounding after the last beat.
So the verse is said in the quiet of early morning, before the day's own drums start up: deadlines, targets, scoreboards. They're allowed to beat. The verse just counts how long each one lasts.

how: Many Sikhs recite this among the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and the nagara, the great kettledrum, is still beaten at some gurdwaras and in Sikh processions.

o: pilgrims who bathed at every holy river
the Sikh armies that held Anandpur
kings who won every land, then still went

p: the remembering that outlasts the march

s: Guru Gobind Singh wrote this verse because he disliked drums and armies
tradition remembers his own great drum, the Ranjit Nagara. he knew the sound of victory, and that it fades.
the verse says the conquerors are beyond counting
kings past, present and to come can't be counted, and without the Name they all still went.
the savaiya says ambition itself is forbidden
it measures the conquerors by whether they remembered the Lord, not by whether they marched.

games.q: you're a king. your drums have carried your name across every land and your horses number in the thousands. what does the savaiya say comes next?
o: without the Name, at the end you go, like the rest.
games.why: the verse lets the drums beat and the elephants trumpet, then follows the kings to their final home. without remembering the Lord, the march ends where every march ends.

practice: Listen for a minute to the sounds around you, near and far, and notice how each one rises and fades.
Then find one small thing you've been pushing for mostly to be seen winning, more likes, the last word, being first, and hold it lightly, like a drumbeat already rolling away.
You don't have to give up every goal; if you pray, say Waheguru as you set this one down.

wordCard.voice: The conquerors. A savaiya of kettledrums and conquered lands: kings beyond counting, who at the end still went without the Name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nagaare, kettledrums, among the drums beating in this savaiya's conquering march.

carryVoice: Your line: drums fade. Remembering keeps sounding. Three hundred sixty-five days: a whole year of days, walked.

sources.ref: Akal Ustat, Tav Prasad Savaiye (the savaiya of conquest with drums, and the savaiya of armored warriors)

sources.work: Sikh historical tradition (e.g., Kesar Singh Chhibber, Bansavalinama; Bhai Santokh Singh, Suraj Granth)
